extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satirical moral essays (early-18th-century literate London audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing short, moralizing satirical essays in the manner of The Spectator: sketch vices and follies, ridicule fashionable affectations, and close with admonition or counsel. Often uses letters, petitions, classical allusions, and ironic mock-forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw vicious characters at length / set them up as a Scarecrow
rubrics_metrics.description: When I meet with any vicious Character that is not generally known, in order to prevent its doing Mischief, I draw it at length, and set it up as a Scarecrow;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extended, concrete sketches of particular characters so they serve as public examples and warnings. The aim is both to expose the person and to 'give Warning to all Her Majesty's Subjects, that they may not suffer by it.' (Use specific incidents and traits rather than vague denunciation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose common social follies as targets
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator enumerates many recurring follies to be corrected: 'our unreasonable Fears and Superstitions... our Fancy for Equipage... our Love of Puppet-Shows... our Notions of Beauty... our Inclination for Romances... our Passion for French Fopperies... our Manhood and Party-zeal... our Abuse of Dancing... our Levity... our Love of Coxcombs... our Tyranny over the Henpeckt' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim satire at widely observed, fashionable, or recurring social vices and affectations so readers recognize the object. The essay lists many specific topical targets (fashion items, entertainments, political affectations) as appropriate material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish satire together with moral counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not only make an Example of the Person to whom it belongs, but give Warning... (and elsewhere urges libertines) 'to take Care of those unfortunate Creatures whom they have brought into the World... to give their spurious Children such an Education... This is the best Atonement they can make.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine ridicule with explicit moral instruction or pragmatic advice: after exposing a vice, offer a corrective, admonition, or constructive remedy rather than mere lampooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exaggerated, humorous remedies or proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Were I to propose a Punishment for this infamous Race... to send them, after the second or third Offence, into our American Colonies... Some Countries punish this Crime with Death; but I think such a Banishment would be sufficient...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ hyperbolic, tongue-in-cheek solutions to spotlight the absurdity of the vice (exaggeration as a satirical device). Present remedies that are intentionally overblown to produce comic contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in varied voices and epistolary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper reproduces many letters and petitions (servants, petitioners, lovers, clergy) as vehicles for humorous and moral points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letters, petitions, testimonials, and mock-forms to present different perspectives, create comic misunderstandings, and let characters reveal folly through their own words. Epistolary pieces allow multiple registers (servant, petitioner, lover) and comedic juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ simile, contrast, and vivid characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: An Enthusiast in Religion is like an obstinate Clown, a Superstitious Man like an insipid Courtier. Enthusiasm has something in it of Madness, Superstition of Folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sharp similes and contrasts to crystallize a vice or character trait (e.g., equating kinds of religious excess to clownish or courtly figures). Vivid, pithy comparisons help make the point memorable and comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical allusion and learned references for authority and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays frequently cite Tacitus, Virg., Apollodorus, Diogenes, Ovid, and other classical sources and references in support of observations or as humorous ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in classical quotations and learned references both to lend authority and to produce literary wit. Allusions can elevate the jest and reward readers who recognize them; they also allow ironic contrast between high learning and low folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony and mock-praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of ironic praise: 'a more flourishing Tree never came out of the Heralds Office' applied to an illegitimate family-tree; mock-complimentary language recurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ irony—praising that which is absurd—to expose vice. Use ostensibly laudatory language that, in context, reveals the author's true critical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt mock-official/legal/petition forms to satirize domestic or social problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Several pieces are framed as petitions ('The humble Petition of John Steward...') or official-sounding complaints to lampoon household spies, voluntary counsellors, and other social nuisances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody bureaucratic or legal language and document forms to ridicule trivial pretensions or to magnify domestic absurdities. The contrast between solemn form and petty content is a source of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue and name particular fashion affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly lists concrete fashion items and affectations (patches, commodes, fans, riding habits, hoop-petticoats, Italian airs in psalm-singing) as examples of follies to be mocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, concrete inventories of fashionable items and practices make satire more pointed and recognizable. Naming particulars rather than speaking in generalities sharpens the comedic attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a moderate, admonitory authorial tone (advocacy of modesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a call to 'value and esteem those who set a moderate Price upon their own Merit' and praise for 'Self-denial' and modesty: 'A modest Man preserves his Character...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an authorial ethos of measured moral seriousness beneath the humor: ridicule excess while upholding moderation as the implicit ideal. The satirist's voice should balance wit with a sense of civic or moral purpose.
